method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders' (vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 2.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC3488504 ('distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0)')). The 2019 first revision (Häberle et al., J Inherit Metab Dis 42:1192–1230, doi:10.1002/jimd.12100) is closed access (Unpaywall: closed; Wiley returned 403) and could not be read, so this guideline uses the open 2012 original.

claims.claim: **UCDs can present acutely or chronically at any age,** often triggered by catabolism, a protein load or some drugs; symptoms are nonspecific (neurological, gastrointestinal, psychiatric). Take a detailed family history with pedigree.
claims.source_text: UCDs may present with acute or chronic presentations at any age and are often triggered by catabolic events, protein load or some drugs. In many cases a precipitating factor cannot be identified. Clinical signs and symptoms are nonspecific and commonly neurological, gastrointestinal or psychiatric. It is essential that healthcare professionals have an awareness of these diseases. Key questions should be asked and a detailed family history with pedigree is mandatory.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Any unexplained encephalopathy or acute psychiatric illness, at any age, must prompt a plasma ammonia.** In a newborn with suspected sepsis, hyperammonaemia is always in the differential.
claims.source_text: UCDs must be included in the differential diagnosis of acute unexplained encephalopathy or acute psychiatric illness at any age, which must prompt plasma ammonia determination. … In newborns with clinical distress where sepsis is suspected, hyperammonemia must always form part of the initial differential diagnosis.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ammonia must be available as an emergency test, with results in 30 minutes.** Measure it for unexplained change in consciousness, unusual neurological illness, liver failure or suspected intoxication.
claims.source_text: Ammonia should be determined in an emergency setting with results available in 30 minutes. … Ammonia should be measured in patients of any age presenting 1) an unexplained change in consciousness; 2) unusual or unexplained neurological illness; 3) liver failure; 4) suspected intoxication.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If ammonia is high, start further metabolic tests immediately, without delaying treatment.** Genetic testing is the first-choice confirmation.
claims.source_text: If ammonia is found elevated, further metabolic investigations should be immediately carried out without delaying specific treatment. … Genetic testing is the method of first choice to confirm the diagnosis.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Do not delay therapy.** Stop protein, start IV 10% glucose, give first-line medications, collect plasma and urine without postponing treatment, and transfer to a specialist centre.
claims.source_text: therapy must not be delayed. Pediatric hospitals should always have first-line medications and consensus-based written protocols on how to proceed. Patients in hyperammonemic crisis should be transferred without delay to a specialist centre after: … 1) stopping protein intake 2) starting intravenous (IV) 10% glucose … 4) plasma and urine collection for diagnostic purposes without postponing treatment initiation.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ammonia scavengers, L-arginine or L-citrulline (and carglumic acid in NAGS deficiency) are the key acute drugs;** watch for toxicity from repeated boluses or high doses of benzoate or phenylacetate. Carglumic acid may also be used in neonatal hyperammonaemia of unknown cause.
claims.source_text: Administration of ammonia scavengers, of L-arginine or L-citrulline and in NAGS deficiency, of carbamylglutamate, is highly valuable for treating acute hyperammonemic decompensation. The potential toxicity of repeated boluses or high doses of benzoate or phenylacetate should be taken into account. … may also be used as an emergency drug during acute neonatal hyperammonemia of unknown etiology.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Dialysis in children when ammonia exceeds 500 μmol/L or there is no response within four hours of medical treatment;** in adults, extracorporeal detoxification is first line. Haemodiafiltration is the method of choice; do not use exchange transfusion.
claims.source_text: In neonates and children with symptomatic hyperammonemia, dialysis should be carried out when ammonia exceeds 500 μmol/L or when there is no response within four hours after starting medical treatment. … Extracorporeal detoxification is the first line treatment in acute hyperammonemic decompensations in adults. … The method of choice for ammonia detoxification is hemodiafiltration. Peritoneal dialysis is a far less effective method. Exchange transfusion should not be used.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep the patient anabolic with high-dose glucose plus lipids** (once a fatty acid oxidation disorder is excluded). Reintroduce protein when ammonia is below 100 μmol/L, ideally within 24–48 hours.
claims.source_text: For treatment of acute hyperammonemia it is crucial to promote and maintain anabolism by infusing high-dose glucose plus lipids (if a fatty acid oxidation disorder has been excluded). Protein should be reintroduced when ammonia returns to <100 μmol/L. Ideally the period of protein-free nutrition should not exceed 24-48 hours.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prognosis is very poor** after more than 3 days of hyperammonaemic coma, clearly raised intracranial pressure, or a peak ammonia above 1000 μmol/L; weigh this before treatment.
claims.source_text: Before treatment of acute hyperammonemia, the prognosis and expected neurodevelopmental outcome must be considered since it can influence the therapeutic decision. Prognosis is considered very poor if: 1. hyperammonemic coma has lasted more than 3 days 2. intracranial pressure is clearly increased 3. ammonia peaked at >1000 μmol/L
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Baby at risk at birth (previous early-onset sibling):** within 30 min start 10% glucose at 4 ml/kg/h; after 4 symptom-free hours give protein-free feeds with oral sodium benzoate and L-arginine 50 mg/kg 6-hourly; check ammonia at 6 h.
claims.source_text: Within 30 min 10% glucose infusion (4 ml/kg/h) should be started and after 4 symptomless hours, protein-free feeds should be given, along with reduction of glucose infusion, and administration of PO 6-hourly 50 mg/kg of both sodium benzoate and L-arginine. Plasma ammonia should be measured at 6 h
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Long-term care rests on:** low-protein diet, essential amino acid supplements, vitamins and minerals, nitrogen-scavenging drugs, an emergency regimen for illness, and liver transplantation for selected patients.
claims.source_text: · low protein diet · essential amino acids supplementation · vitamin and mineral supplementation · medications to increase waste nitrogen excretion · caring for special situations and provision of emergency regimen in intercurrent illnesses · liver transplantation for selected patients.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diet needs a specialist metabolic dietitian;** FAO/WHO/UNU figures guide protein and energy. When natural protein tolerance is too low, give 20-30% of total protein as essential amino acids (up to 50% in arginase deficiency), split over 3 or 4 meals.
claims.source_text: Dietary treatment is a cornerstone of therapy. This warrants the particular expertise of a specialist metabolic dietitian to finely balance nutritional requirements with metabolic stability. The FAO/WHO/UNU recommendations can be used to guide the protein and energy requirements. … A reasonable approach [] is to provide 20-30% of the total protein intake as EAA supplements, except in ARGD1, when supplements of EAA can, if necessary, be increased to 50% of total protein because of the severity of protein restriction (see below). EAA's should be given as an equally divided dose with 3 or 4 main meals to enhance utilisation and prevent nitrogen overload.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Take oral sodium benzoate and sodium phenylbutyrate 4-times daily with meals and plenty of fluid** to avoid mucositis or gastritis. Give written drug sheets to parents, pharmacists and carers.
claims.source_text: To avoid mucositis or gastritis, oral sodium benzoate and sodium PBA (as granules, tablets, or undiluted liquid preparations) should be taken 4-times daily during meals with abundant fluids. … Written drug treatment sheets should be provided to parents, pharmacists and persons involved in patient care.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sodium phenylbutyrate side effects:** menstrual dysfunction or amenorrhoea in ~25% of postpubertal females, reduced appetite, taste disturbance, body odour and branched-chain amino acid depletion.
claims.source_text: Sodium PBA causes menstrual dysfunction/amenorrhea in ~25% of postpubertal females [], and can decrease appetite, disturb taste and cause disagreeable body odour. Also it may deplete BCAAs and increase the risk of endogenous protein catabolism
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor plasma arginine in everyone;** except in arginase deficiency, most need L-arginine or L-citrulline, aiming for fasting arginine about 70–120 μmol/L in ASS and ASL deficiency.
claims.source_text: All UCD patients should be monitored for plasma arginine levels. Except in ARG1D, most will need L-arginine or L-citrulline supplementation. … In these patients fasting plasma arginine concentrations should be about 70-120 μmol/L
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Carglumic acid is the first-line treatment for NAGS deficiency.** Give carnitine 25–50 mg/kg/d only if plasma carnitine deficiency is proven.
claims.source_text: N-carbamyl-L-glutamate is the first line medication for treatment of NAGSD … In cases of proven plasma carnitine deficiency 25-50 mg/kg/d carnitine should be given.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start the emergency regimen without delay (even at home) when illness threatens hyperammonaemia;** call the metabolic unit if there is no prompt improvement. Vaccinate on the normal schedule; treat fever above 38°C.
claims.source_text: If there is an immediate risk of hyperammonemia as a consequence of an intercurrent illness or other event, the emergency regimen (Table 6) should be started without delay, even at home. … If there is no prompt improvement the metabolic unit should be contacted urgently … Vaccinations do not substantially increase the risk of decompensations and are recommended at the same schedule as for healthy children. If temperature exceeds 38°C antipyretic treatment should be started.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Elective surgery only when fully well, in a centre that can manage hyperammonaemia;** switch drugs to IV and infuse 10% glucose the day before.
claims.source_text: elective surgery should be undertaken when the patient is completely well including no minor intercurrent illness and has normal ammonia/amino acid levels. Surgery should only be carried out in centres prepared for dealing with acute hyperammonemic decompensations. The day before surgery drug treatment should be switched to IV and glucose (10%) infused to ensure anabolism.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Liver transplantation is the only cure;** ideally before irreversible neurological damage, generally between 3 and 12 months of age, for severe neonatal onset (not NAGS deficiency), progressive liver disease, recurrent crises despite treatment, or poor quality of life.
claims.source_text: The only available curative treatment for UCDs is liver transplantation, allowing return to a normal diet and stopping drug administration. … Liver transplantation should ideally be carried out before irreversible neurological damage and/or repeated crises, generally between 3 and 12 months of age. It may be considered in all patients (excepting NAGSD) with severe neonatal onset. It is also indicated for patients with progressive liver disease (e.g. ASLD), for those suffering recurrent metabolic decompensations and hospitalisations despite medical therapy, as well as those with poor quality of life.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Targets:** ammonia below 80 μmol/L, glutamine below 1000 μmol/L, arginine high-normal, and essential and branched-chain amino acids normal. Test IQ and development regularly.
claims.source_text: Venous ammonia and amino acid levels should be monitored, aiming at levels of ammonia <80 μmol/L, glutamine <1000 μmol/L, arginine in the high normal range and EAAs and BCAAs in the normal range. … Regular testing for IQ, development and specific abilities/weaknesses is recommended.
claims.locator: Häberle J, Boddaert N, Burlina A, et al. (European UCD guideline group, E-IMD), Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases, 'Suggested guidelines for the diagnosis and management of urea cycle disorders', vol. 7, article 32, published 29 May 2012, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3488504/, retrieved 2026-09-23
